ICT.title: Introduction to Information and Communication Technology
ICT.summary: A comprehensive overview of ICT, covering its definition, historical periods from premechanical to electronic, personal computers, and the evolution of the World Wide Web and social media.
ICT.content:
Definition and Overview of ICT

Information and Communication Technology (ICT) refers to the technologies, including both hardware and software, that enable humans to communicate with one another. It is a specific form of technology designed to facilitate communication. The history of ICT is categorized into four main historical periods: Premechanical, Mechanical, Electromechanical, and Electronic.

1. The Premechanical Period (3,000 BCE to 1,450 CE)

This era represents the earliest roots of communication and information processing.

  • Early Communication: Humans began using symbols as substitutes for words.
  • Storage Media: While stone tablets were the initial medium, they were eventually abandoned for being too heavy and bulky.
  • Papyrus Plant: This led to the first production of paper, which revolutionized how information was stored.
  • Libraries: These establishments are considered the first data centers in human history.
  • The Abacus: Introduced by the Romans in the 2nd Century BCE but originating from China, it was the first counting device and the first device used to process information. It was a manual device similar in function to a modern calculator.

2. The Mechanical Period (1450–1840)

This period focused on machines that could enhance the speed and efficiency of calculations.

  • Pascaline: A mechanical calculator invented by Blaise Pascal and Wilhelm Schickard.
  • Analytical Engine: Invented by Charles Babbage in 1837, who is known as the 'Father of the Computers'. It featured an arithmetic logic unit (ALU), integrated memory, and control flow (composed of loops and conditional branching). These specific features became the blueprint for the development of computers in the first half of the 20th century.

3. The Electromechanical Period (1840–1940)

This era ushered in a new age by using electricity for long-distance communication.

  • Telegraph: Invented in 1837 by William Cooke and Sir Charles Wheatstone, it is considered the first electrical communications device. The first working model utilized five magnetic needles that pointed to letters and numbers via an electric current.
  • Morse Code: Invented by Samuel Morse in 1844 for use with the single-circuit telegraph; it is a system still utilized in various industries today.
  • Telephone: Invented by Alexander Graham Bell (patent granted in 1876), it converted sound into electricity for transmission over copper wires.
  • The Bombe: Invented by Alan Turing in 1939 and improved by Gordon Welchman in 1940, this device was used to decipher German encryption codes during World War II.

4. The Electronic Period (1940s to Present)

This current era is focused on the advent of solid-state and electronic devices.

  • Four Main Events: This period includes the late vacuum tube era, the transistor era, the integrated circuit era, and the computer processor era.
  • ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer): The first electronic, general-purpose computer. It was a massive machine occupying 167 square meters.
  • Transistor: Invented in 1947 as a faster, lightweight alternative to vacuum tubes, it serves as the foundation for all modern electronics.
  • Integrated Circuit (IC): A single package composed of a group of transistors and circuit elements.
  • Personal Computers: Olivetti Programma 101 (1965) was designed by Pier Giorgio Perotto and his team as the first commercial personal computer sold. IBM 5150 (1981) was developed by a team led by Don Estridge and set the standard for modern PC platforms.

Modern ICT and the World Wide Web

The modern ICT network is a fusion of hardware, software, Graphical User Interfaces (GUI), and communication networks.

  • World Wide Web (WWW): Proposed by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989, it is the system that allows users to access hypertext documents and files over the internet.
  • Evolution of the Web: Web 1.0 is the 'read-only' Web. Web 2.0 is the 'read-and-write' Web, which allowed for interactivity, e-mail interaction, and social networking. Web 3.0 is the 'semantic executing' Web, envisioned to be smarter, faster, and capable of a wider range of searches.
  • Social Media: These high-impact applications emerged with Web 2.0 for socializing in virtual communities.
  • Virality: Defined as the rate at which information, media, or ideas are shared or reposted on social media profiles.

COMP.title: Computers: Uses, Function, Characteristics, and Applications
COMP.summary: An overview of computer uses, basic functions, distinguishing characteristics, and diverse field applications based on Module 2.
COMP.content:
I. Uses of Computers

Computers serve several primary roles in modern society, including:

  • Research and Information Retrieval: Accessing and gathering data.
  • Communication: Connecting with others globally.
  • Entertainment: Providing various forms of digital leisure.
  • Business Operations Tool: Used for records management, word processing, and report generation.

II. Computer Functions

The computer operates through a cycle of four main functions:

  • Input: Receiving data in the form of words, symbols, numbers, sounds, pictures, or program instructions.
  • Process: The microprocessor or CPU calculates, sorts, and modifies data.
  • Output: Delivering results (such as reports, graphs, documents, or pictures) via a printer or monitor.
  • Store:
    • Memory (RAM): A temporary holding area for data.
    • Storage (Disk): Permanent data retention.

III. Characteristics of a Computer

Computers possess specific traits that distinguish them from human processing:

  • Speed: They perform calculations at incredible rates. For example, the CM-5 (1993) could perform 131 billion operations per second, a task that would take a human with a calculator 41,000 years.
  • Memory: Computers can store and recall every piece of information accurately, only 'forgetting' if specifically asked to delete data.
  • Diligence: Computers do not suffer from tiredness or lack of concentration.
  • Versatility: They adapt easily to different subjects and occupations, remaining skilled across many objects (though the source mistakenly labels this under 'Memory').
  • Accuracy: While errors can occur, they are typically caused by human weaknesses—such as imprecise thinking by programmers or incorrect data entry—rather than technological failure.

IV. Applications in Different Fields

Computers affect nearly every sector of the 'Computer Age':

  • Engineering & Architecture: Used for animated experiments and visual 'walk-throughs' of proposed buildings to improve design accuracy and speed.
  • Education: Enhanced classroom learning and the introduction of new teaching methods that help students learn faster than traditional methods.
  • Government: Used for weather forecasting, park management, processing immigrants, producing social security checks, and collecting taxes.
  • The Home: Tasks include record-keeping, writing letters/memos, budgeting, producing presentations, and connecting with the rest of the planet.
  • Health and Medicine: Monitoring critically ill patients in intensive care units and providing cross-sectional views of the body.
  • Manufacturing Industries: Performing dangerous or unpleasant jobs, such as deep-earth mining or explosive device disposal.
  • Connectivity: Assisting and aiding individuals with physical and mental disabilities.
  • Scientific Research: Propelling research forward for the benefit of mankind.
  • Communication: Facilitating cheap and popular global connections via the World Wide Web.
  • Paperwork: Reducing manual paperwork across millions of industries, making management faster and more effective.

V. Future Vision

As technology evolves, the integration of computers will become more seamless. Bill Gates has noted that in the coming years, 'the conference table will be a computer, the whiteboard will be a computer'.

HW.title: Computer Hardware
HW.summary: A comprehensive guide integrating fundamental computer operations, cycles, characteristics, and detailed definitions of computer hardware components from input devices to storage and communication.
HW.content:
Part I: The Role and Nature of Computers

Definition: A powerful tool used for research, communication, and business operations like record management and report generation.

Basic Functions (The Cycle)

  • Input: Receiving data (words, symbols, numbers, etc.).
  • Process: The CPU calculates and modifies that data.
  • Output: Delivering results via monitors or printers.
  • Storage: Holding data temporarily (RAM) or permanently (Disk).

Key Characteristics (Exceeding Human Capacity)

  • Speed: Performing billions of operations per second.
  • Memory: Accurately storing and recalling vast amounts of data without 'forgetting.'
  • Diligence: Maintaining focus and accuracy without tiredness.
  • Versatility: Adapting to various subjects and occupations.
  • Accuracy: Errors are typically due to human input (programmers/data entry) rather than the machine itself.

Part II: Detailed Computer Hardware & Definitions

Definition of Hardware: Physical devices that enable the input, processing, output, storage, and communication of data.

1. Input Devices

Purpose: Accept data and instructions from users or other systems.

  • Keyboard: A typewriter-like device used to enter commands.
    • Alphanumeric Keypad: Used for typing letters, numbers, and punctuation.
    • Numeric Keypad: Keys (0–9 and math symbols) used for calculating and cursor movement.
    • Cursor Keys: Arrow keys and navigation buttons like Page Up/Down, Home, and End.
    • Function Keys: Keys at the top (F1–F12) for special program functions.
    • Special Keys: Escape (quick exit), Caps Lock (capital letters), Shift (uppercase/symbols), Ctrl & Alt (combination keys), Enter (execute), and Backspace (erase left).
    • Status Lights: Indicators for Num/Caps/Scroll Lock.
  • Pointing Devices:
    • Mouse: A box-like device that controls the cursor through pointing, clicking, double-clicking, dragging, or right-clicking.
    • Trackball: A stationary device where the user rotates a ball to move the pointer.
    • Light Pen: A light-sensitive detector used to select objects by pointing directly at the screen.
  • Specialised Input:
    • Touch Screen: A touch-sensitive transparent panel for finger-based input.
    • Touch Tablet: A surface used by designers and artists for drawing.
  • Scanning Devices: Barcode Readers (read codes via light rays), Wand Readers (laser-based), and Scanners (translating printed media into digital form).
  • Media Capture: Digital Cameras (capture snapshots as bit patterns) and Audio Digitizers (digitize sound from microphones).
  • Sensing Devices: Monitor physical properties like temperature, pressure, and humidity.

2. The System Unit & Processing Hardware

System Unit: The electronic circuitry housing where processing occurs.

  • External Components: Power Switch, Reset Switch (restarts without power-off), Casing (protective shell), LEDs (status lights), and Ports (holes for data transfer).
  • The Microprocessor (CPU): Known as the heart or brain of the computer.
    • Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): Performs math and logic comparisons.
    • Control Unit (CU): Directs the entire CPU operation (fetching, decoding, executing).
    • Registers: Temporary data holding places for passing information between instructions.
  • Internal Motherboard Components:
    • Motherboard: The main circuit board containing the CPU, memory, and ports.
    • Memory Slot: A socket for memory modules.
    • Chipsets: Integrated circuits designed to work together for specific functions.
    • Cache Memory: A high-speed buffer smaller than main storage that stores likely next-use instructions.
    • Jumpers: Electrical contact prongs on the motherboard or cards.
    • Processor Socket: The location holding the CPU chip.
    • BIOS Chip: The hardware-to-OS interface; manages settings and booting.
    • CMOS Chip: Battery-powered chip holding the real-time clock and BIOS settings.
  • Support Hardware: Expansion Cards (Sound, Video, Network, Game, Memory), Hard Disk (giant internal storage), Power Supply (processing power), Fan (cools the CPU), and Internal Speaker.

3. Output Devices

Purpose: Translate processed data into human-readable forms.

  • Monitor: A television-like display.
    • CRT Monitor: Uses pixels; large size and high power consumption.
    • Flat-Panel Monitor: Reduced weight and power (includes Emissive like LED/Plasma or Non-Emissive like LCD).
    • Color Types: Monochrome (two colors), Gray-Scale (shades of gray), and Color/RGB (red, green, blue signals).
  • Print Devices: Produce printed output on paper.
    • Kinds: Dot-matrix (uses hammers), Ink-jet (sprays ink), and Laser (uses laser beams and a rotating drum for high-quality prints).
    • Sizes/Speeds: 80 column or 132 column paper widths; 9 Pin Serial or the faster 24 Pin Parallel printers.
  • Audio/Graphic Output: Speakers (electrical-to-sound), Plotters (finely scaled engineering drawings), and Synthesizers (electronically generated sounds).

4. Storage Devices

Functions: Reading (transferring data from medium to memory) and Writing (memory to medium).

  • Primary Storage (Main Memory): Temporary area known as RAM (Random Access Memory), which is erased when power is lost. ROM (Read Only Memory) is "Permanent Memory" for basic operations.
  • Secondary Storage Types:
    • Magnetic: Uses magnetized particles (e.g., Floppy Disks, Hard Disks, Zip Disks, and Tape Drives).
    • Optical: Uses pits on a surface (e.g., CD-ROM and DVD-ROM).
    • Magneto-Optical: Allows rewriting (e.g., CD-R and CD-RW).
    • Solid-state: Uses non-volatile memory arrays (e.g., Memory Cards).

5. Communication Devices

  • NIC (Network Interface Card): Physically connects a computer to a network.
  • Modem: Modulator/Demodulator that exchanges info over phone lines. Available as Internal (motherboard card) or External (stand-alone serial port device).

SW.title: Computer Software
SW.summary: A comprehensive guide to computer software, covering its core definitions, main classifications (system vs. application software), productivity tools, software utilities, financial/business software, graphics and multimedia software, specialized industry applications, educational/entertainment software, and distribution models derived from the provided sources.
SW.content:
I. Fundamental Software Definitions

Software refers to a set of instructions, also called programs, that tells the computer what to do or how to perform specific tasks. These instruction sets provide a means for users to interact with and use the computer. While hardware is tangible, software represents the intangible side of technology. The computer consists of two basic types of software: system software and application software.

II. System Software vs. Application Software

A. System Software

System software helps run the computer and coordinates instructions between application software and the computer's hardware devices. It includes:

  • Operating System (OS): Manages overall system operation and coordinates hardware and software components.
  • Utility Programs: Programs (often built into the OS) that help manage system resources. Examples include floppy drive formatters, antivirus software (scans files to detect and remove malicious software or viruses), and compression software (reduces file size to save storage space and speed up transmission).
  • Device Drivers: Specialized programs that enable communication between the OS and specific hardware devices.
  • Middleware: Provides connectivity and services between applications beyond what the OS provides.

B. Application Software

Application software includes programs used to perform specific tasks at home, school, and work. Categories include productivity software, specialty software, entertainment software, educational/reference software, and personal software.

III. Application Software Categories

A. Productivity Software

Productivity software includes programs that enable users to perform various tasks required for creating, managing, and analyzing data:

  • Word Processing Software: Used to create and edit written documents. Features include quick and easy editing, a variety of formatting options, graphics, and templates. Examples include Microsoft Word, Google Docs, and Corel WordPerfect.
  • Spreadsheet Software: Used to perform calculations and numerical analyses. Features include worksheets with cells, values, formulas, functions, and automatic recalculation. Includes built-in mathematical functions like SUM(), PRODUCT(), QUOTIENT(), MOD(), MIN(), and MAX(). Examples include Microsoft Excel and Lotus 1-2-3.
  • Presentation Software: Used to create dynamic presentations. Features include slide layouts, preformatted design templates/backgrounds, animation effects (controlling how text and objects enter/exit), slide transitions, and viewing modes like Normal/Slide view. Examples include Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides, and Corel Presentations.
  • Database Software / Database Management Systems (DBMS): Complex electronic filing systems used to store, retrieve, and manage structured information. Data is organized into fields (a data category), records (a collection of related fields), and tables (groups of related records). Examples include Microsoft Access and Corel Paradox.
  • Personal Information Manager (PIM) Software: Strives to replace traditional desk management tools like calendars, address books, notepads, and to-do lists, often incorporating email management. Examples include Microsoft Outlook and Lotus Organizer.

B. Productivity Software Tools

  • Wizards: Step-by-step guides that walk users through the necessary steps to complete a complicated task by asking interactive questions.
  • Templates: Pre-designed forms included with software that provide the basic structure for a document, spreadsheet, or presentation.
  • Macros: Small programs that group a series of commands to run as a single command, best used to automate routine tasks or complex command sequences.

C. Integrated Applications vs. Software Suites

  • Integrated Software Applications: Incorporate the most commonly used tools of many productivity programs into one integrated standalone program without complex advanced features. Example: Microsoft Works.
  • Software Suites: Bundled collections of standalone programs packaged together. Available for productivity, graphics, and virus protection in various application combinations. Examples include Microsoft Office, Lotus SmartSuite, and WordPerfect Office.

IV. Financial and Business-Related Software

A. General Categories

Grouped into personal financial software, general business software, and specialized business software.

B. Key Types

  • Tax-preparation Software: Enables users to prepare taxes independently with complete forms, instructions, and expert advice. Examples: Intuit TurboTax and H&R Block TaxCut.
  • Financial Planning Software: Helps manage daily finances with electronic checkbook registers and automatic bill payment tools. Examples: Intuit Quicken and Microsoft Money.
  • Accounting Software: Helps small business owners track accounts receivable/payable, inventory management, payroll, and billing. Examples: QuickBooks and Peachtree Accounting.

V. Graphics and Multimedia Software

  • Graphics Software: Wide range of programs used by home users and professionals to design documents, images, illustrations, and Web pages.
  • Multimedia Software: Includes video and audio editing, animation, and game production tools.
  • Image-editing (Photo-editing) Software: Enables editing photographs and images (e.g., removing red-eye, modifying color hues, removing scratches/rips). Examples: Adobe Photoshop, Canva, and Picasa.
  • Drawing (Illustration) Software: Used to create or edit 2D line-based drawings, technical diagrams, nonphotographic drawings, animations, and illustrations. Examples: Adobe Illustrator, Microsoft Visio, and MS-Paint.
  • Desktop Publishing (DTP) Software: Allows creative layout and arrangement of graphics and text in documents. Examples: QuarkXPress and Adobe PageMaker.
  • Video-editing Software: Edits digital videos using special effects, transitions, narration/voiceover, and overlays. Examples: Adobe Premiere and Microsoft Movie Maker.
  • Digital Audio Software: Uses MP3 compression for audio files. Features include MP3 recording (direct capture from streaming audio/mics), ripping (copying CDs to MP3 format), and MP3 burning (recording MP3s onto a CD).
  • Web Page Authoring Software: Enables users to design interactive Web pages without HTML knowledge. Examples: Macromedia Dreamweaver and NVU.
  • Computer-aided Design (CAD) Programs: 3D modeling tools used by engineers for automated designs, technical drawings, and model visualizations.

VI. Specialized Business Tasks and Industry Software

  • Project Management Software: Creates and modifies scheduling charts to plan/track tasks and coordinate resources. Example: Microsoft Project.
  • Mapping Programs: Used for travel-intensive businesses. Example: Rand McNally StreetFinder.
  • Customer Relationship Management (CRM) Software: Centralized database for storing sales and client contact information. Example: GoldMine.
  • Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) Systems: Controls back-office operations like billing, production, inventory, and HR management.
  • Vertical Market Software: Industry-specific software (e.g., Master Builder for construction, real estate property management, library automation).
  • Proprietary Software: Custom-developed software owned and controlled by a specific company.

VII. Educational, Reference, and Entertainment Software

  • Entertainment Software: Primarily consists of computer games and virtual reality programs that turn artificial environments into realistic experiences.
  • Educational Software: Instructional tools, including course management software for web-based classes featuring calendars, grade books, and discussion boards. Examples: WebCT, Blackboard, and Moodle.
  • Reference Software: Digital source materials like atlases, dictionaries, and thesauri.
  • Personal Software: Compiles and organizes data stored across your computer.

VIII. Software Licensing, Distribution, and Development

  • Software License: Legal agreement granting rights to use software under specific terms.
  • Freeware: Fully free software (e.g., Facebook, Instagram).
  • Shareware: Provided free for a trial period (e.g., Canva).
  • Beta Version: Pre-release software undergoing testing before public launch (e.g., Wild Rift deployment).
  • Open Source: Software with source code freely accessible, editable, and redistributable online.
